method: The water temperature is the target dough temperature multiplied by the number of temperatures being averaged — 3 for a straight dough of water, flour and room, 4 when a preferment also counts — minus the flour temperature, the room temperature, the preferment temperature when used and the friction rise. The result is the water temperature that makes the mixed dough average out to the target, because the finished dough settles near the average of the temperatures that went into it. Every degree moved on the water moves the dough by one degree divided by the factor count, and cooler flour or a cooler room allows warmer water. The friction rise is the heat mixing itself adds and depends on the mixer type, the dough mass, the speeds and the mixing time, so it has to be measured for the equipment in use rather than assumed; published figures run from roughly 3 °C by hand to 13 °C on a planetary stand mixer. A required water temperature below 0 °C cannot be met with liquid water, so the flour must be chilled or part of the water replaced with ice. Values are refused outside 1 to 45 °C for the target, −20 to 50 °C for the flour, room and preferment temperatures and 0 to 30 °C for the friction rise, and decimal commas are accepted. The page does not estimate fermentation time, judge whether dough is proofed or make any food-safety claim, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: The desired dough temperature formula multiplies the target by 3 for a straight dough or 4 when a preferment is used, then subtracts the flour, room, preferment and friction temperatures to give the required water temperature.

The friction factor is the temperature rise caused by mixing and varies with the mixer, dough mass, speed and mixing time; measured examples run from about 6–8 °F by hand to 22–24 °F on a planetary stand mixer.
The preferment version of the formula multiplies the desired dough temperature by four and subtracts the preferment temperature along with the room, flour and friction temperatures.
